say.text: A 2-month-old, not diagnosed before birth, is pink and feeding well. There is a loud harsh systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border. Echo confirms tetralogy of Fallot (TOF).
What best explains a pink baby with TOF?

choices.label: Moderate obstruction: he is a 'pink Tet'
The echo is wrong; TOF is always blue from birth
He is in a spell, so the murmur is loud

say.text: Ask what decides how much blood gets forced past the lungs. The note ties the presentation to one thing.
Tempting: TOF is the classic blue baby, and it most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate.
But 'most commonly' is not 'always'. This baby is well apart from a loud murmur. What does that suggest about the degree of obstruction?

sure_note.text: You were sure, so pause here: 'most common' is a frequency, not a rule for every child.

say.text: Tempting: a harsh loud murmur sounds like trouble. But this baby is pink and feeding well, and a spell is a deeply blue event.
Ask what level of obstruction leaves a baby well apart from a loud murmur.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note it: a loud murmur on its own does not mean a spell.

say.text: Same baby: pink, feeding well, loud murmur, TOF on echo. Which explanation fits?

choices.label: Moderate obstruction: he is a 'pink Tet'
The echo is wrong; TOF is always blue from birth
He is in a spell, so the murmur is loud

say.text: Different angle: the obstruction can be moderate. Such infants, if not diagnosed before birth, may be asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur, and are called 'pink Tets'.
So the picture is the answer: pink and well with a loud murmur means moderate obstruction, not a spell and not a wrong echo.
Yes. Moderate RVOT obstruction in an infant not diagnosed before birth may leave only a loud murmur: a 'pink Tet'.
The rule behind it: when resistance across the RVOT is less than systemic vascular resistance, the child is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.
Picture a seesaw: RVOT resistance on one end, systemic resistance on the other. Blood takes the easier way.
Months later this baby's obstruction becomes significant. Predict his colour.

choices.label: He turns blue: most blood now bypasses the lungs
He stays pink: 'pink Tet' is a fixed type of TOF
He turns blue because pulmonary vascular resistance has risen

say.text: Right. With significant RVOT obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
Presentation varies with how severe the obstruction is, so 'pink' describes a degree, not a separate disease.
Tempting: 'pink Tet' sounds like a category. But it was described for infants with moderate obstruction, and the balance depends on RVOT resistance versus systemic resistance.
When obstruction becomes significant, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed: he turns blue.

Tempting: pulmonary resistance sounds like the lungs' fault. But the balance in this note is resistance across the RVOT against systemic vascular resistance, and the presentation varies with RVOT obstruction.
With significant obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
A friend writes this in her notes. Which line is safe to write for the exam?

choices.label: Most common cyanotic CHD; most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate
Every child with TOF is cyanotic from birth
Most common cyanotic CHD, so most blue neonates have TOF

say.text: Yes. TOF is the most common cyanotic congenital heart disease, and it most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate.
Both hold, and pink Tets still exist.
Tempting: the first line is true, so 'always' feels like a small step. But pink Tets are asymptomatic apart from a loud murmur.
The safe wording: most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate.
Tempting: it swaps the direction of the pair. The source says TOF is the most common cyanotic CHD, and that TOF most commonly presents as a cyanotic neonate.
Keep the two statements separate: one ranks TOF among cyanotic CHD, the other describes how TOF presents.
Now listen to a 6-month-old with TOF at the left upper sternal border.
Which auscultation fits?

choices.label: Harsh ejection murmur, pulmonary S2 component inaudible
Harsh ejection murmur, loud pulmonary S2 component
Harsh ejection murmur, widely split S2

say.text: Yes. The murmur is harsh systolic ejection, best heard at the left mid to upper sternal border with posterior radiation, and the pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible.
Tempting: 'pulmonary' lesions bring to mind a loud P2. But in TOF the pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible.
Blood bypasses the pulmonary bed when obstruction is significant, so little reaches that valve.
Tempting: splitting is the usual S2 story in right-sided lesions. But in TOF the pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible, so there is little to split.
The murmur itself is harsh systolic ejection at the left mid to upper sternal border.
Back to the same child at 4 months. He has been crying hard, turns deeply blue and breathes fast. Agitation can trigger a tet spell.
Before you listen, predict: how does the systolic murmur change during the spell?
Do not use the usual rule yet. In this moment, where is the blood going: across the RVOT or toward the aorta?
Tempting: the greater the obstruction, the more prominent the murmur.
Hold that rule and ask where the blood is going right now, in the middle of a spell.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so this is worth a second look: a rule from the resting state does not automatically hold during a spell.

say.text: Tempting: the anatomy has not changed, so the murmur should not either. But the child's state has changed: he is blue and breathing fast.
Ask where the blood is going right now.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so note: a spell is a change in flow, not in anatomy.

say.text: Same child, deep in the spell. How does the murmur change?
Trace it. With significant obstruction, most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed. Less blood crosses the RVOT, so less noise.
That is why the intensity of the murmur decreases during a tet spell, even though at rest more obstruction means a more prominent murmur.
Yes. During a tet spell the intensity of the murmur decreases.
Why: most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed, so less crosses the RVOT. At rest, more obstruction means a more prominent murmur.
Two weeks later, a doctor lists TOF findings. Which one does NOT fit?

choices.label: A loud pulmonary component of S2
An inaudible pulmonary component of S2
A murmur that softens during a spell

say.text: Right. The pulmonic component of S2 is usually inaudible in TOF, so a loud one does not fit.
Tempting: an inaudible P2 sounds like a missing finding, not a feature. But it is the usual finding in TOF.
The one that does not fit is the loud pulmonary component.
Tempting: a quieter murmur sounds like a lesser problem. But during a tet spell the murmur's intensity decreases.
The finding that does not fit is the loud pulmonary component of S2, since P2 is usually inaudible.
A mother says: 'Doctor, last week you heard a loud murmur; today it is almost gone, so he must be better.' The baby is deeply blue and crying.
What is going on?

choices.label: A hypercyanotic spell: less blood crosses the RVOT
The murmur is unrelated to his blue colour

say.text: Yes. A fall in murmur intensity during a tet spell goes with blood bypassing the pulmonary bed, not with relief.
Tempting: at rest, a softer murmur would mean less obstruction, since more obstruction gives a more prominent murmur.
But in a spell the intensity decreases because most blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
Tempting: murmur and colour feel like separate signs. But they share one cause: significant RVOT obstruction sends most blood toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
During a spell the murmur's intensity decreases as the child turns blue.
